title: Records: transparent carriers for data
goal: By the end you can write a record whose compact constructor validates and normalizes every instance, explain what javac generates for it, and say exactly where its equality and immutability stop.

warmup.q: `record Masked(String card)` overrides its accessor so that `card()` returns `"****1111"` for the card 4111111111111111. What does `toString()` return?
options: `Masked[card=****1111]`, because toString calls the accessor
Nothing: it doesn't compile, because record accessors can't be overridden
`Masked@1b6d3586`, because overriding an accessor turns off the generated toString
warmup.why: The generated `toString`, `equals` and `hashCode` read the private field directly, not the accessor, so the full number reaches the log. Overriding an accessor is legal as long as the return type matches. To hide a component, override `toString` itself, as the lab does.

sections.h: Equality and immutability go one level deep
sections.body:
`equals` on a record returns true when the other object is the same record class and every component is equal. For a reference component that means `Objects.equals`. For a primitive it means the wrapper's `compare` returns 0, which has two surprises for a `double`. A record holding `NaN` equals another one holding `NaN`, though `NaN == NaN` is false. And `0.0` and `-0.0` are not equal, though `0.0 == -0.0` is true. Kotlin data classes behave the same way. Keep money in a `long` of minor units and neither will bite you.

Arrays are worse. An `int[]` component compares by reference, so two records with equal arrays are not equal, and `toString` prints something like `[I@1b6d3586`. Use a `List`.

A `List` component brings the real trap. The record holds a reference to whatever list the caller passed in, and if the caller keeps changing that list, the record changes too:

```java
record Batch(String id, List<String> paymentIds) {}

var ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay_1", "pay_2"));
var batch = new Batch("b-7", ids);
var sent = new HashSet<>(Set.of(batch));
ids.add("pay_3");
sent.contains(batch);              // false: the hashCode changed under the set
```

```kotlin
data class Batch(val id: String, val paymentIds: List<String>)

val ids = mutableListOf("pay_1", "pay_2")
val batch = Batch("b-7", ids)
val sent = hashSetOf(batch)
ids += "pay_3"
batch in sent                      // false: the hashCode changed under the set
```

The batch is still in the set. The set just looks for it in the wrong bucket. The fix is one line in the compact constructor: `paymentIds = List.copyOf(paymentIds);`. It makes an unmodifiable copy, and it throws `NullPointerException` for a null element. That is what you want for domain data, and a surprise for JSON lists that contain nulls. Kotlin's `List<String>` is a read-only view, not an immutable list, so a data class needs the same copy, made in a factory. *Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal* in the concurrency track made the same point about sharing between threads. Here the cost is a lost key, even on one thread.

The last trap looks like a fix. To keep a card number out of the logs, someone overrides the accessor so `card()` returns `****1111`. The logs don't change. The generated `toString` reads the field directly (that is what the getters in the bootstrap arguments are), so it still prints the full number. The override also breaks the record contract that `new Masked(m.card())` equals `m`. Record patterns, which lesson 3 covers, do call the accessor, so different parts of your code now see different data. To hide a component, override `toString`, or keep the secret out of any record that gets logged.

sections.h: Records, data classes and the missing copy()
sections.body:
Kotlin engineers reach for `copy()` first and find Java has none. A record that needs "the same refund with a smaller amount" gets a hand-written wither:

```java
record Refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor, List<String> reasons) {
    Refund withAmount(long newAmount) {
        return new Refund(paymentId, newAmount, reasons);   // through the canonical constructor
    }
}
```

```kotlin
data class Refund(val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long, val reasons: List<String>)

val part = full.copy(amountMinor = 2_000)                  // generated, and it runs init
```

Both go through validation, which is the point: there is no path to an invalid `Refund`. The cost on the Java side is typing, and it grows with the record. In a 2020 design draft, Brian Goetz pointed out that while a class has O(n) getters, it "could conceivably have O(2^n) withers", and asked that hand-written withers not become a best practice. Write withers only for the changes your domain actually makes.

A language fix exists on paper. JEP 468, derived record creation, proposes `refund with { amountMinor = 2_000; }`. It would take the record apart, run the block, and call the canonical constructor with the result. It is a Candidate JEP, no JDK has shipped it, and in January 2026 Goetz wrote that it "has been 'on hold' for a while". Don't plan around it.

The other differences matter more day to day. A data class may declare properties in its body, and Kotlin leaves those out of `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString` and `copy()`, so two objects that differ only there are equal. A record can't have body state at all. A data class can't be `open`, `abstract` or `sealed`, and a record is always final. Kotlin destructures with `val (id, amount) = refund`, through `componentN()` functions, while Java destructures with record patterns in `switch` and `instanceof` (lesson 3).

Where the two languages meet, Kotlin reads a Java record's accessors as properties (`money.minor`), and `@JvmRecord` on a data class emits a real `java.lang.Record` that Java code sees as one. The Kotlin docs warn that adding `@JvmRecord` to an existing class is not a binary-compatible change, so decide when you create the class.

try.title: Wither versus copy()
steps: Run `WitherDemo` and its twin `WitherDemoKt`. Compare the four lines each prints.
Add a `withPaymentId(String id)` wither to the Java record and call it with `" "`. Should that be rejected? Add the check where every wither will get it.
In `WitherDemo.kt`, add `var note = ""` to the body of `RefundRequest`, set `full.note = "called twice"`, and print `full == full.copy()` and `full.copy().note`.

code.title: WitherDemo.java

alt.title: WitherDemo.kt

try.expect: Both versions print the original, the changed refund, `same reasons list object: true` and a rejected negative amount. Withers and `copy()` both reuse the component references, which is safe here only because the list can't change. The blank-id check belongs in the compact constructor, so every wither inherits it. In Kotlin, `full == full.copy()` is `true` and the copy's `note` is empty: body properties are ignored by `equals` and not copied.

analogy: A record is like a line on a printed bank statement: date, amount, reference. Anyone can read every field, two lines with the same values mean the same thing, and to change one you print a new line. The bank checks the line before it prints it, which is the compact constructor's job. The analogy breaks at one point: a printed line can't point at anything that changes later, while a record's `List` component can be someone else's list that keeps growing after the record was made.
in_your_world: Your Quarkus services already move records around: REST request and response bodies, Kafka event payloads, Temporal activity inputs. Each of those is a boundary where outside data becomes a value, and the compact constructor is where you check it once: three-letter currency codes, non-negative amounts, idempotency keys of the right length. After that, any `Money` the service holds is a valid one. Two places need care. A `List` component in a Kafka event must be copied, or a producer that reuses its buffer list changes events it has already handed off. And a record that holds a PAN, an IBAN or an access token must override `toString`, because the generated one prints every component into every log line and exception message that touches the record.
mistake: The common mistake is treating a record as deeply immutable and using it as a map or set key while one of its components is a mutable list or map. It works in tests, because nothing mutates the list there. In production a caller reuses its `ArrayList`, the record's `hashCode` changes, and `HashMap.get` returns null for a key that is still in the map. Copy every collection component in the compact constructor with `List.copyOf`, `Set.copyOf` or `Map.copyOf`, and don't use arrays as components.

compare.title: A validated money value in Java and Kotlin

java.title: Money.java

kotlin.title: Money.kt

compare.note: Both give you `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` over all components, final fields, and a validation hook that every construction goes through, including Kotlin's `copy()`. Three things differ. Java's compact constructor can normalize a parameter before it becomes a field; a data class can only reject it, so normalizing lives in a factory and the public constructor stays open to raw input. Java deserialization rebuilds a record through its canonical constructor but skips a data class's `init` (`@JvmRecord` closes that gap). And Kotlin has `copy()` with named arguments, while Java has hand-written withers until JEP 468 ships, which it hasn't.

worked.title: Turn a mutable request class into a record

steps.say: A capture request in a payment service is a JavaBean: setters, a mutable list, and sixty lines of hand-written `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` that nobody updated when `currency` was added. Any code can change it after it was checked.

Write the header. The components are the whole state, and every setter is gone. Recompile: each place that called a setter is now a compile error, which is your list of code that mutated a request after it was built.
steps.code:
// 1. the components are the state
public record CaptureRequest(String paymentId, Money amount, List<String> lineItems) {}
steps.alt_code:
// 1. the properties are the state
data class CaptureRequest(val paymentId: String, val amount: Money, val lineItems: List<String>)

steps.say: Add the compact constructor. Reject what can't be valid, then copy the list so the caller can't change it later. `amount` is a `Money`, which validates itself, so the request doesn't repeat those checks.

Add only the wither the domain needs. Partial captures happen, so `withAmount` earns its place. It calls the canonical constructor, so a partial capture can't skip the checks. In Kotlin, `copy(amount = ...)` already exists and runs `init`.
steps.alt_code:
// 4. no wither to write: copy() is generated and runs init
    val partial = request.copy(amount = Money.of(2_000, "eur"))

Order matters in `Money`: normalize first, then check for three letters, or `" eur "` fails the check.

drill.title: A validated key from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `record IdempotencyKey(String value)` that rejects null, trims the value, and then rejects anything that isn't 16 to 64 letters, digits or `-`. Then write the Kotlin version. Which of the two can store the trimmed value without a factory?

recap: A record is a final class with private final fields, public accessors, one canonical constructor and generated `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. It can't add instance fields or extend a class.
Validate and normalize in the compact constructor. Every path goes through it: `new`, factories, other constructors, withers and Java deserialization.
Equality compares every component: `Objects.equals` for references and `compare` for primitives, so `NaN` equals `NaN` and `0.0` doesn't equal `-0.0`. Arrays compare by reference.
Records are only shallowly immutable. Copy collection components with `List.copyOf`, or a mutated key gets lost in a `HashSet`.
The generated methods read fields, not accessors. To hide a secret, override `toString`.
Kotlin has `copy()` and Java has hand-written withers, because JEP 468 is on hold. Java deserialization skips a data class's `init` unless the class is `@JvmRecord`.

quiz.q: `record Batch(String id, List<String> ids)` is a key in a `HashMap<Batch, Status>`. The producer that built it later calls `ids.add("pay_9")` on its own list. What does `map.get(batch)` most likely return now?
options: The status, because records are immutable
`null`, because the key's hashCode changed and the map looks in the wrong bucket
It throws ConcurrentModificationException
The status, because HashMap compares record keys with ==
quiz.why: The record's fields are final, but the list they point to is the producer's list. `hashCode` includes the list, so it changes, and the map searches a bucket where the entry isn't. Nothing throws. Copying the list in the compact constructor prevents it.

quiz.q: Which of these makes `new Money(5, "usd")` equal to `new Money(5, "USD")`?
options: `public Money { this.currency = currency.toUpperCase(); }`
`public String currency() { return currency.toUpperCase(); }`
`public Money { currency = currency.toUpperCase(); }`
`public Money(long minor, String currency) { currency = currency.toUpperCase(); }`
quiz.why: In the compact form you reassign the parameter and javac assigns the field afterwards. Assigning `this.currency` doesn't compile. The accessor override leaves the fields different, and `equals` compares fields. The full canonical constructor in the last option never assigns the fields, so it doesn't compile either.

quiz.q: A Kotlin `data class Range(val lo: Int, val hi: Int) : Serializable` checks `lo <= hi` in `init`. A cache deserializes a tampered stream that says lo = 5, hi = 1. What happens?
options: You get `Range(lo=5, hi=1)`: Java deserialization doesn't run `init`
`InvalidObjectException`, because `init` runs during deserialization
`IllegalArgumentException` from `require`
`ClassCastException`, because the stream no longer matches the class
quiz.why: Java deserialization builds a plain serializable class without calling its constructor, so `init` never runs and the invalid object comes back. A Java record, or the same data class marked `@JvmRecord`, is rebuilt through its canonical constructor, and the stream is rejected with `InvalidObjectException`.

quiz.q: From the memory model track: `record RateCard(Map<String, Long> fees)` copies the map with `Map.copyOf` in its compact constructor. A new `RateCard` is published through a plain, non-volatile field. What is guaranteed for a thread that reads the new reference?
options: Nothing: without volatile it may see a null map
It may see a half-built map
Nothing, because records have no final fields
It sees the map as the constructor left it, because record fields are final, though it may keep reading the old reference for a while
quiz.why: Record fields are private final, so final-field semantics apply: a thread that sees the reference sees the fields, and the map built in the constructor, as the constructor left them. A plain field doesn't promise when the new reference becomes visible. Publish it through a volatile field if readers must see updates promptly.

quiz.q: `data class Payment(val id: String) { var status = "NEW" }`. Payment `a` has status NEW, payment `b` has the same id and status CAPTURED. What is `a == b`?
options: `false`, because the statuses differ
`true`
It doesn't compile: data classes can't have body properties
It depends on which object was created first
quiz.why: Only primary-constructor properties take part in a data class's `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString` and `copy()`. `status` lives in the body, so Kotlin ignores it. A Java record can't have body state at all, so the question can't arise there.

flashcards.front: What does javac generate for `record Point(int x, int y)`?
flashcards.back: Private final fields, accessors `x()` and `y()`, a canonical constructor `Point(int, int)`, and `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. The class is final and extends `java.lang.Record`.

flashcards.front: In a compact constructor, how do you normalize a component?
flashcards.back: Reassign the parameter: `currency = currency.trim();`. javac assigns the fields after the body. `this.currency = ...` doesn't compile.

flashcards.front: A record overrides its accessor to mask a card number. What does `toString` print?
flashcards.back: The full number. The generated `toString`, `equals` and `hashCode` read the fields, not the accessors. Override `toString` instead.

flashcards.front: `record R(double d)`: is `new R(Double.NaN).equals(new R(Double.NaN))` true?
flashcards.back: Yes. Primitive components compare with `Double.compare`, which treats NaN as equal to itself. And `0.0` doesn't equal `-0.0`.

flashcards.front: How do you make a record with a `List` component safe as a map key?
flashcards.back: Copy it in the compact constructor: `items = List.copyOf(items);`. The copy is unmodifiable and rejects null elements.

flashcards.front: Does Java deserialization run a Kotlin data class's `init` block?
flashcards.back: No, so a tampered stream can build an invalid object. A Java record, or a data class marked `@JvmRecord`, is rebuilt through its canonical constructor.

flashcards.front: Can you write `refund with { amount = 200; }` in Java today?
flashcards.back: No. Derived record creation (JEP 468) is a Candidate JEP, on hold as of January 2026, and in no JDK. Write withers by hand.

terms.plain: One of the values in a record's header. Each one gets a private final field and a public accessor.
The constructor whose parameters match the components in order. Every other way of making the record goes through it.
The canonical constructor written without a parameter list. Its parameters are locals you can check and reassign; javac assigns the fields at the end.
The generated public method that returns a component. It is named after the component: `currency()`, not `getCurrency()`.
The fields can't be reassigned, but the objects they point to may still change.
A method that returns a copy of a record with one component changed. Java has no generated ones.
A Kotlin annotation that compiles a data class to a real `java.lang.Record`.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate says: "Our `Payout(String iban, long amount, List<String> tags)` record is immutable, so it's safe to keep in a `HashSet` and to log as it is." Explain, in your own words, the two ways that can go wrong and what you would change.
explain_back.answer: A record is only shallowly immutable. Its fields can't be reassigned, but `tags` points to whatever list the caller passed, and if the caller keeps changing that list the record's `hashCode` changes and the set can't find it any more. Copy the list in the compact constructor with `List.copyOf`. Logging is the second problem: the generated `toString` prints every component, so the full IBAN goes into the logs. Overriding the `iban()` accessor doesn't help, because `toString` reads the field directly. Override `toString` and print a masked IBAN there.
